questions.q: Why can survey data never be a perfectly objective truth?
a: It reflects what people report, so bias can enter during collection
Statistical software cannot handle large samples
People always lie about their age and income
Samples are usually too small to calculate averages
questions.why: Lesson 1 says much data comes from questionnaires and focus groups, so the result represents the study.

questions.q: What detail did media reports about the coffee and heart disease study leave out?
a: That benefits were found only for two to three cups a day, not other amounts
That the study was never actually published
That the researchers were funded by tea companies
That coffee had no effect on any group
questions.why: Lesson 2 explains the study only showed benefits at two to three cups, saying nothing about other amounts.

questions.q: Why does the media tend to exaggerate findings?
a: To attract clicks, shares and web traffic
To make complicated studies easier to replicate
To protect readers from uncertain results
To pressure journals into publishing faster
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the media overstates data to increase click-through rates and sharing.

questions.q: What does the summary say about the link between coffee and productivity?
a: Coffee drinkers may simply work in jobs where productivity is rewarded
It proves that caffeine directly improves concentration
It shows productivity causes people to drink coffee
It is impossible to study in any reliable way
questions.why: Lesson 3 uses this example to show a correlation can have a third explanation behind it.

questions.q: What does the summary advise when you see dramatic data in the news?
a: Check the source and consider how the data was collected and displayed
Assume the numbers are fabricated and ignore them
Trust it if the headline includes a percentage
Share it quickly before the study is retracted
questions.why: Lesson 2 concludes that you should check sources carefully because presentation shapes interpretation.
